## Overview

In this hands on exercise, we learn how to build information dashboard in R.

By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

-  create bullet charts using **ggplot2**

-  create sparklines using **ggplot2**

- build an industry standard dashboard using **R Shiny**


## Getting Started

### Installing and Loading Packages

In this hands on exercise, four R packages will be used. 


| Package | Description |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) | A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org/), [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/), [tidyr](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/), [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/)), [tibble](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/),[stringr](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/),[forcats](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/), and [purr](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/)|
| [gtExtras](https://jthomasmock.github.io/gtExtras/index.html) | Provides additional helper functions that make it easier to create visually appealing tables with gt. The [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com/) package is designed to help users produce well formatted and attractive tables in R. |
| [ggthemes](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggthemes/index.html) | Provides 'ggplot2' themes and scales that replicate some of the famous looks. |
| [lubridate](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lubridate/index.html) | A Tidyverse package that handles date-time objects |
| [reactable](https://glin.github.io/reactable/index.html) | Provides functions for creating interactive data tables in R, built on the [React Table](https://github.com/tanstack/table/tree/v7) library and implemented through [reactR](https://github.com/react-R/reactR).|
| [reactablefmtr](https://kcuilla.github.io/reactablefmtr/index.html) | Offers a range of features that simplify and improve the styling of interactive reactable tables, providing easy to use and highly customisable functions and themes.
|


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(lubridate, ggthemes, reactable,
reactablefmtr, gt, gtExtras, tidyverse)
```
:::


## Importing Microsoft Access Database

### The data set

For the purpose of this study, a personal database in Microsoft Access *mdb* format called **Coffee Chain** will be used.

### Importing database into R

In the code chunk below, `odbcConnectAccess()` from the [RODBC](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RODBC/index.html) package is used to import a database query table into **R**.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(RODBC)
con <- odbcConnectAccess2007('data/Coffee Chain.mdb')
coffeechain <- sqlFetch(con, 'CoffeeChain Query')
write_rds(coffeechain, "data/CoffeeChain.rds")
odbcClose(con)
```
:::



 An **.mdb** file is a Microsoft Access database file that stores tables, queries, and other database objects.

Next, `sqlFetch()` is used to retrieve the table named *CoffeeChain Query* from the database. The retrieved data is returned to R as a data frame.

Finally, `write_rds()` is used to save the data frame as an **.rds file**. This format stores a single R object efficiently and allows the dataset to be quickly reloaded later using `read_rds()` for further analysis.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::kable(head(coffeechain, 10))
```

### Data Preparation

The code chunk below is used to import *CoffeeChain.rds* into R.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
coffeechain <- read_rds("data/CoffeeChain.rds")
```
:::


The code below aggregates Sales as `current` and aggregates Budgeted Sales as `target`  by Product by using `group_by()`, `summarise()` and `ungroup()` from **dlpyr** package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `current` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()         
```
:::


### Bullet chart in ggplot2


There are two types of bar charts in **ggplot2**: `geom_bar()` and [`geom_col()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html).

**`geom_bar()`** sets the height of each bar based on the number of observations in each category. If a **weight** aesthetic is provided, the height represents the sum of the weights.

In contrast, **`geom_col()`** uses the actual values from the dataset to determine the height of the bars. Therefore, it is appropriate when the values to be displayed are already computed.

We finally have a good example of `geom_col()` here. The dataset has the prepared **current** and **target** values for each product. The code belpw creates a bar plot that compares the current performance with the target. Different background shades and bar widths are used to represent the target ranges and the current value, forming a cool **bullet chart** style visualisation. The wider grey bars indicate the target thresholds, while the narrower black bar represents the current value.

[`geom_errorbar()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_linerange.html) is cleverly designed here to draw a vertical red line as target value for each product. Because the minimum and maximum values are set to the same value (target), the error bar collapses into a line that serves as a reference marker rather than showing variability.

Now we can easily pinpoint which products meet their targets and which do not.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(product, aes(Product, current)) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, max(target) * 1.01),
           fill = "grey85", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.75),
           fill = "grey60", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.5),
           fill = "grey50", width = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, current), width = 0.35, fill = "black")+
   geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,x = Product, min = target, ymax= target), 
                width = .4,colour = "red",linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Product", y = "Current Sales", title  = "Coffee Chain Product Sales Dashboard") +
 theme(axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

:::
:::

:::callout-tip

In ggplot2, `coord_flip()` only changes the visual orientation (such as axis ticks, labs), but the scales still refer to the original mapping.


:::


## Plotting sparklines using ggplot2

In this section, we learn how to plot sparklines by using **ggplot2**.


### Preparing the data

The code chunk below prepares the monthly sales report from 2013 onward by filtering the date, creating a month column, grouping the data by product and month, and calculating the total sales before ungrouping the data.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sales_report <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date)) %>%
  group_by(Month, Product) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)
```
:::

The code below creates three grouped data frames to identify the minimum and maximum sales for each product by month, using `group_by()` together with `slice(which.min())` and `slice(which.max())`. It also extracts the latest monthly sales for all 13 products.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mins <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.min(Sales))
maxs <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  slice(which.max(Sales))
ends <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>%
  filter(Month == max(Month))
```
:::



The code below creates the 25th and 75th percentile (quantile) columns using `quantile(var, 0.25)` and quantile`(var, 0.75)`, and then joins the results to the sales report using a `right_join()` to keep all rows from *sales_report*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
quarts <- sales_report%>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(quart1 = quantile(Sales, 0.25),
            quart2 = quantile(Sales, 0.75)) %>%
  right_join(sales_report)
```
:::

### Sparklines in ggplot2

The code below creates sparklines using `geom_line()`, with a shaded background added via `geom_ribbon()`. It also uses `geom_point()` to highlight the minimum and maximum values, and annotates the end values with labels. Although **ggplot2** sparklines are flexible, the resulting plot can be difficult to read, particularly for product names and their corresponding values.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x = Month, y = Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(data = quarts, aes(ymin = quart1, max = quart2), fill = 'grey90') +
  geom_line(size = 0.3) + 
  geom_point(data = mins, col = 'red') +
  geom_point(data = maxs, col = 'blue') +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) + 0.25* (max(sales_report$Month) -min(sales_report$Month))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 12, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 3) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), strip.text = element_blank())
```

## Static Information Dashboard Design: gt and gtExtras methods

In this section we learn how to create a static dashboard using the [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com/) and [gtExtras](https://jthomasmock.github.io/gtExtras/index.html) packages. It is recommended to review their official documentation to gain a general understanding of their features and functionality before getting started.


### Plotting a simple bullet chart

Creating build chart with in a table is quite straightforward using **gt** and **gtExtra** packages. First, we use the [`gt()`](https://gt.rstudio.com/) function from the **gt** package to create a `gt` table object. The [`gt_plt_bullet()`](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/gtExtras/html/gt_plt_bullet.html) from **gtExtra** package is then used to generate a bullet chart, where the **current** value is compared **against** a **target** value. By default, the palette displays the bar in grey and the target marker in red. In this case, the colours are customised to light blue for the bar and black for the target. Additionally, the [`gt_theme_538()`](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/gtExtras/html/gt_theme_538.html) function **gtExtra** package is used to apply **FiveThirtyEight** theme which alternates the column background colours between grey and white.

Similar to **ggthemes**, other gtExtra themes `gt_theme_dark()`, `gt_theme_espn()`, `gt_theme_excel()`, `gt_theme_guardian()`, `gt_theme_nytimes()`, `gt_theme_pff()` are also available. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_bullet_table <- function(data, theme = "538") {
  
  theme_fun <- switch(
    theme,
    "538" = gtExtras::gt_theme_538,
    dark = gtExtras::gt_theme_dark,
    espn = gtExtras::gt_theme_espn,
    excel = gtExtras::gt_theme_excel,
    guardian = gtExtras::gt_theme_guardian,
    nytimes = gtExtras::gt_theme_nytimes,
    pff = gtExtras::gt_theme_pff,
    stop("Invalid, select one of: dark, espn, excel, guardian, nytimes, pff")
  )
  
  data %>%
    gt::gt() %>%
    gtExtras::gt_plt_bullet(
      column = current,
      target = target,
      palette = c("lightblue", "black")
    ) %>%
    theme_fun()
}
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_bullet_table(product, "espn")
```

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report <- coffeechain %>%
  mutate(Year = year(Date)) %>%
  filter(Year =="2013") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(Product, Month) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup()
```
:::

It is important to note that most functions in the gtExtras package require the input data frame to include list columns. Accordingly, the following code chunk transforms the report data frame into a structure with list columns to ensure compatibility with these functions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise('Month Sales' = list(Sales), .groups = "drop")
```

### Plotting *coffechain* sales report

The code below plot sparklines for the monthly sales for each product by using [`git_plt_sparline()`](https://jthomasmock.github.io/gtExtras/reference/gt_plt_sparkline.html) from **gtExtra** package. Other plottings include `gt_plt_bar_pct()`, `gt_plt_bar_stack()`,` gt_plt_dist()`, `gt_plt_percentile()`, `gt_plt_point()`, `gt_plt_sparkline()`, `gt_plt_winloss()`.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise('Monthly Sales' = list(Sales), .groups = "drop") %>%
  gt() %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`, type = "ref_iqr", #referene line
                   fig_dim = c(5,50), #height/width of the plot
                   # palette = c("black", rep("transparent", 4)), #show no points
                   same_limit = FALSE) # individual axis range
```

:::callout-tip

- `type`: A string indicating the type of plot to generate, accepts "default", "points", "shaded", "ref_median", 'ref_mean', "ref_iqr", "ref_last". "points" will add points to every observation instead of just the high/low and final. "shaded" will add shading below the sparkline. The "ref_" options add a thin reference line based off the summary statistic chosen.

- `palette`: A character string with 5 elements indicating the colors of various components. Order matters, and palette = sparkline color, final value color, range color low, range color high, and 'type' color (eg shading or reference lines). To show a plot with no points (only the line itself), use: palette = c("black", rep("transparent", 4)).

:::


### Adding statistics

The code below calculates the minimum, maximum, and average sales while removing missing values using `na.rm = TRUE`. It then creates a *gt* table and formats the numerical values to two decimal places using [`fmt_number()`](https://gt.rstudio.com/reference/fmt_number.html) from **gt** package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise("Min" = min(Sales, na.rm = T), "Max" = max(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Average" = mean(Sales, na.rm = T)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = 4, decimals = 2) # column average
```

###  Combining the data.frame with sparklines


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
spark <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales), .groups = "drop")

sales <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise("Min" = min(Sales, na.rm = T), "Max" = max(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Average" = mean(Sales, na.rm = T))
sales_data = left_join(sales, spark)
```
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sales_data %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = 2:4, decimals = 0) %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`, same_limit = FALSE, type = 'shaded')
```

### Combining bullet chart and sparklines
 
Here we create a data frame with filtered and total actual and toal target sales and left join with sales data. 

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bullet<- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`Target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `Actual` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()
sales_data = left_join(sales_data, bullet)
```

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sales_data %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = 2:4, decimals = 0) %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`,same_limit = FALSE,type = "shaded", fig_dim = c(5,45)) %>%
  gt_plt_bullet(
    column = Actual,target = Target,width = 30,palette = c("lightblue", "black")) %>%
  cols_label(Actual = "Actual*") %>%
  gt_theme_nytimes() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Coffee Chain Sales Report, 2013") %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*The back bar marks the total sales target.") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = "small", align = "right"),
                              locations = cells_source_notes())
```

## Interactive Information Dashboard Design: reactable and reactablefmtr methods

In this section, we learn how to create an interactive information dashboard using the [**reactable**](https://glin.github.io/reactable/) and [**reactablefmtr**](https://kcuilla.github.io/reactablefmtr/) packages.
To enable the creation of interactive sparklines, the [**dataui**](https://timelyportfolio.github.io/dataui/articles/dataui_reactable.html) package needs to be installed, as shown in the code chunk below. The interactive table with sparklines looks cool and sleek which might be useful to our CPI project dashboard. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
remotes::install_github("timelyportfolio/dataui")
```
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(dataui)
```
:::


###  Plotting interactive sparklines

To create interactive sparklines in **reactablefmtr**, we first need to aggregate the monthly sales and store them as `list` columns. This is because the function works on vectorised values. This approach is similar to what we did earlier with **gtExtras**.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales))
```
:::


[`reactable()`](https://glin.github.io/reactable/articles/examples.html) from the **reactable** package constructs an interactive table with features such as scrolling, sorting, and filtering.` colDef()` is used to define how individual columns are displayed in a reactable.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
reactable(sales) 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

Next, we create a `reactable` object using `reactable()` and integrate sparklines using [`react_sparkline()`](https://kcuilla.github.io/reactablefmtr/reference/react_sparkline.html).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
 report %>%
  reactable(.,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(.,
        height = 50, show_line = TRUE, line_color = "black",statline = "mean",
        statline_color = "red", bandline = "innerquartiles", bandline_color = "darkgreen"
      )
    )
  )
)
```

### Changing the pagesize


Here, we use [`defaultPageSize()`](https://glin.github.io/reactable/reference/reactable.html) from **reactable** to display 13 rows per page, so there is no need to navigate to a second page. By default, the table displays 10 rows.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
 report %>%
  reactable(.,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(.,
        height = 50, show_line = TRUE, line_color = "black",statline = "mean",
        statline_color = "red", bandline = "innerquartiles", bandline_color = "darkgreen"
      )
    )
  )
)
```

### Adding points and labels

We add the `highlight_points` argument to `react_sparkline()` to highlight the minimum and maximum values. We also use `labels = c("first", "last")` to label the first and last points in the sparkline.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  reactable(
    .,
    defaultPageSize = 13,
    columns = list(
      Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
      `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
        cell = react_sparkline(
          .,
          height = 50,
          show_line = TRUE,
          line_color = "black",
          bandline = "innerquartiles",
          bandline_color = "darkgreen",
          highlight_points = highlight_points(min = "red", max = "blue"),
          labels = c("first", "last")
        )
      )
    )
  )
```

### Adding reference line

Next, we use the `statline` argument to display a reference line (e.g. mean) in the sparkline. Other available options include `"mean", "median", "min", and "max"`, with the default colour Red. The `statline_label_size` argument controls the size of the label shown next to the reference line, with a default value of `"0.8em"`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  reactable(
    .,
    defaultPageSize = 13,
    columns = list(
      Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
      `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
        cell = react_sparkline(
          .,
          height = 50,
          show_line = TRUE,
          line_color = "black",
          bandline = "innerquartiles",
          bandline_color = "darkgreen",
          highlight_points = highlight_points(min = "red", max = "blue"),
          statline = "mean", statline_color = "grey", statline_label_size = '0.7em'
        )
      )
    )
  )
```

### Adding bandline

As explored earlier, we can also add a `bandline` to display a horizontal band that highlights ranges of interest. Available options include `"innerquartiles"` and `"range"` (from minimum to maximum). The colour of the band can be customised using bandline_color, with the default set to red.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report %>%
  reactable(
    .,
    defaultPageSize = 13,
    columns = list(
      Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
      `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
        cell = react_sparkline(
          .,
          height = 50,
          show_line = TRUE,
          line_color = "black",
          bandline = "innerquartiles",
          bandline_color = "darkgreen",
          statline = "mean",
          statline_color = "grey",
          statline_label_size = "0.7em",
          highlight_points = highlight_points(
            first = "red",
            last  = "blue"
          )
        )
      )
    )
  )
```

### Changing from sparkline to sparkbar

Another useful function is [`react_sparkbar()`](https://kcuilla.github.io/reactablefmtr/reference/react_sparkbar.html), which is similar to react_sparkline() in terms of its arguments.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkbar(
        report,
        highlight_bars = highlight_bars(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        statline = "mean")
    )
  )
)
```
